main.title: Gauntlet
main.summary: Gauntlet is a 1985 dungeon crawl maze video game developed and published by Atari Games for arcades.

cards.heading: A dungeon designed for shared play
cards.text: Gauntlet is a 1985 dungeon crawl maze video game developed and published by Atari Games for arcades. It is one of the first multiplayer dungeon crawl arcade games. The core design of Gauntlet comes from the 1983 game Dandy for the Atari 8-bit computers, which resulted in a threat of legal action. It also has similarities to the 1983 maze game Time Bandit.

cards.heading: Finding room for four players
cards.text: The arcade version of Gauntlet was released in October 1985, initially available only as a dedicated four-player cabinet. Atari distributed a total of 7,848 arcade units. In Japan, the game was released by Namco in February 1986. Atari later released a two-player cabinet variant in June 1986, aimed at operators who could not afford or did not have sufficient space for the four-player version.

main.title: Xanadu
main.summary: Xanadu, also known as Xanadu: Dragon Slayer II, is an action role-playing game developed by Nihon Falcom and released in 1985 for the PC-8801, X1, PC-8001, PC-9801, FM-7 and MSX computers.

cards.text: Xanadu, also known as Xanadu: Dragon Slayer II, is an action role-playing game developed by Nihon Falcom and released in 1985 for the PC-8801, X1, PC-8001, PC-9801, FM-7 and MSX computers. Enhanced remakes were later released for the Sega Saturn, PC-9801 and Windows platforms. It is the second entry in the Dragon Slayer series, preceded by Dragon Slayer and followed by Dragon Slayer Jr: Romancia, which, as most games in the Dragon Slayer series, have little relation with each other.

Xanadu set a sales record for computer games in Japan, with over 400,000 copies sold there in 1985. It was one of the foundations of the role-playing genre, particularly the action role-playing subgenre, featuring real-time action combat combined with full-fledged character statistics, innovative gameplay systems such as the Karma meter and individual experience for equipped items, and platform game elements combined with the dungeon crawl gameplay of its predecessor. It also had towns to explore and introduced equipment that change the player character's visible appearance, food that is consumed slowly over time and is essential for keeping the player character alive, and magic used to attack enemies from a distance.
The following year saw the release of Xanadu Scenario II, an early example of an expansion pack. The game spawned the Xanadu series, a spin-off from the Dragon Slayer franchise.

main.title: Golden Joystick Awards 1986
main.summary: The Golden Joystick Awards, with every category winner of the 1986 edition.

cards.heading: The players' awards
cards.text: The Golden Joystick Awards celebrate games through a public vote, bringing players into the choice of each year's winners. The awards began in Britain with the 1983 season and later reached an international audience through online voting. Their changing categories trace the growth of games: home computers and consoles, handhelds, online play, independent studios, performance and music. Alongside the public vote, special honours recognise individual contributions to the industry. Each edition preserves its own category names, so the results also show what players and the awards organisers considered worth celebrating at the time.

main.title: Tehkan World Cup
main.summary: Tehkan World Cup, originally released as World Cup in Japan, is an association football video game released by Tehkan (now Tecmo) to arcades in 1986, following location testing in late 1985.

cards.text: Tehkan World Cup, originally released as World Cup in Japan, is an association football video game released by Tehkan (now Tecmo) to arcades in 1986, following location testing in late 1985. It features multiplayer gameplay and trackball controllers. It was released in both upright and table arcade cabinets, but was most commonly released in a cocktail cabinet form factor. Its arrival coincided with the buildup to the 1986 FIFA World Cup. It featured the then colors of several of the world's top teams such as West Germany, Argentina and Brazil, although it did not mention any team by name.

The game uses a bird's-eye view, with the trackball controls allowing game physics such as controlling both the direction and speed of the shot. The gameplay format was adapted from the American football game Gridiron Fight, developed by the same team and released earlier in the year, for an association football game, but with the controls simplified down to a trackball and single action button. It became a major success in arcades, and was a landmark title for association football games upon release. While Tehkan World Cup was not officially ported to home systems at the time, its gameplay format was later adapted by Sensible Software to develop the home computer game MicroProse Soccer (1988) and provided the basis for later association football games such as the Sensible Soccer series in the early 1990s.

In 1990, Tehkan World Cup was ported to the Nintendo Entertainment System as Tecmo World Cup Soccer. The original arcade version was also released for the PlayStation 2 and Xbox consoles as Tecmo Cup in the 2000s.

main.title: Out Run
main.summary: Out Run is a 1986 racing video game developed and published by Sega for arcades.

cards.text: Out Run is a 1986 racing video game developed and published by Sega for arcades. It is known for its pioneering hardware and graphics, nonlinear gameplay, a selectable soundtrack with music composed by Hiroshi Kawaguchi, and the hydraulic motion simulator deluxe arcade cabinet. The goal is to avoid traffic and reach one of five destinations before time runs out.

Out Run was designed by Yu Suzuki, who traveled to Europe to gain inspiration for the stages. Suzuki's original concept was to base it on the 1981 American film The Cannonball Run, of which he was a fan. He disliked racing games in which cars exploded on impact, and wanted gamers to enjoy the experience of driving and to feel "superior".

Suzuki had a small team and only ten months to program Out Run, leaving him to do most of the work himself. It was a critical and commercial success, becoming the highest-grossing arcade game of 1987 worldwide, as well as Sega's most successful arcade cabinet of the 1980s. It was ported to numerous video game consoles and home computers, becoming one of the best-selling video games at the time and selling millions of copies worldwide. Out Run is considered one of the greatest games and is cited as an influence upon numerous games, playing a role in the arcade industry's recovery, and providing the name for a subgenre of synthwave. It was followed by several sequels, beginning with Turbo OutRun in 1989.

main.title: Ikari Warriors
main.summary: Ikari Warriors, known as Ikari in Japan, is a 1986 run and gun video game developed and published by SNK for arcades.

cards.text: Ikari Warriors, known as Ikari in Japan, is a 1986 run and gun video game developed and published by SNK for arcades. It was released in North America by Tradewest. Amongst the numerous Commando clones on the market, Ikari Warriors was distinguished by its unique control style with rotary joysticks and a two-player cooperative mode. The rotary joystick controls were in turn based on SNK's earlier TNK III (1985). Ikari was originally intended to be an official licensed adaptation of the film Rambo: First Blood Part II (1985), but SNK were initially unable to acquire the rights to the film.

The game was a major commercial success in arcades. It was Japan's second highest-grossing table arcade in 1986, and London's third highest-grossing arcade game that year. It was also a major breakthrough US release for SNK, ranking among America's top five highest-grossing dedicated arcade games for two years in a row, in 1986 and 1987.

main.title: The Legend of Zelda
main.subtitle: Freedom Begins with a Map Without Arrows
main.summary: The Legend of Zelda first appeared in Japan in 1986 for the Famicom Disk System.

cards.heading: A way into Hyrule
cards.text: The Legend of Zelda first appeared in Japan in 1986 for the Famicom Disk System. Link's journey joins an overworld of woods, mountains and caves to a series of dungeons. The opening offers a place to enter and directions to try rather than a single track to the finish.

cards.heading: Remember a place, return with a tool
cards.text: A new item can change the meaning of an earlier obstacle. Bombs, a raft or another acquired tool give the player reasons to revisit locations and test a suspicion. Progress depends partly on keeping a mental map: where something was seen can matter as much as which enemy was defeated.

cards.heading: An adventure kept for later
cards.text: The original disk release could record progress, and the later NES cartridge used battery-backed memory. Saving suited a world intended to be explored over more than one sitting. These are different physical versions of the same idea: the adventure could still be there when the player returned.

cards.heading: Before the labyrinth, a sheet of paper
cards.text: Nintendo's preserved development plans show Zelda's dungeons as arrangements of rooms on paper. Their positions establish routes, connections and places the player may need to revisit. A secret on screen begins as something deliberately placed in that layout. These drawings reveal the planning behind an adventure experienced as exploration.

main.title: Atlus
main.subtitle: From contract development to Shin Megami Tensei
main.summary: Atlus was founded on April 7, 1986 by a team of six, initially doing contract development.

cards.heading: Atlus and the Risk of Staying Recognizable
cards.text: Atlus was founded on April 7, 1986 by a team of six, initially working on contract development. It later became closely associated with Shin Megami Tensei and Persona. Its catalogue spans internal development, publishing and collaborations, through changes in ownership and corporate structure. Demon negotiation, fusion and social relationships would become some of the systems most closely linked with its role-playing games.

cards.heading: Six People and Contract Work
cards.text: The company's official timeline begins with six people and contract projects. Working for other companies preceded the development of a widely recognised Atlus catalogue. These early commissions built the technical experience and business relationships on which later projects depended.

cards.heading: Shin Megami Tensei Turns Systems into a Position
cards.text: Shin Megami Tensei, released in 1992, lets players negotiate with demons, recruit them and combine them through fusion. Building a party involves choosing which abilities to keep and which creatures to sacrifice for a new result. Moral alignments and alliances connect these decisions to the direction of the story. Party development and the player's position in the world become closely related.

cards.heading: Persona: relationships that strengthen the party
cards.text:
In the Persona series, Personas are physical manifestations of a person's psyche and subconscious used for combat.

"Social Links" is a system introduced in Persona 3 that is a form of character interaction tied to the growth of Personas. During their time outside battle, the main character can interact with and grow a particular Social Link, which acts as an independent character growth system tied to a Persona family or Arcanum. As the main character's relationship with the character representing a Social Link grows, its rank is raised and more powerful Personas related to the Social Link's assigned Arcanum can be summoned and fused. Attributes related to the main character's social life can also be used to improve their Persona abilities, such as their academic abilities and social aptitude. An enhanced version of the Social Link system, known as "Confidants", appeared in Persona 5.

main.title: Ninja Kid
main.summary: Ninja Kid, known in Japan as GeGeGe no Kitaro - Yōkai Daimakyō (GeGeGe no Kitaro: The Evil Yōkai Realm), is an action video game developed by Tose and published by Bandai for the Nintendo Entertainment System.

cards.text: Ninja Kid, known in Japan as GeGeGe no Kitaro - Yōkai Daimakyō (GeGeGe no Kitaro: The Evil Yōkai Realm), is an action video game developed by Tose and published by Bandai for the Nintendo Entertainment System.

The Japanese version was based on the 1985 television series GeGeGe no Kitarō itself based on the manga series of the same name, but the game was changed to the generic "Ninja Kid" and all references to Kitaro were removed for the American version due to the source material being not well-known outside Japan.

This game was followed by a sequel titled Gegege no Kitarou 2: Youkai Gundan no Chousen, which was released the following year only in Japan also by Bandai; however, that title was a role-playing video game and its plot is unrelated to the original.
It was the eighth best-selling Famicom game of 1986, selling 1,250,000 copies.

main.title: Dragon Quest
main.subtitle: Dragon Quest Teaches Console Players How to Read a Role-Playing Game
main.summary: Yuji Horii, Akira Toriyama and Koichi Sugiyama helped make computer role-playing approachable on a console.

cards.heading: Dragon Quest Teaches Console Players How to Read a Role-Playing Game
cards.text: Enix released Dragon Quest for the Famicom in Japan on May 27, 1986. Yuji Horii, artist Akira Toriyama, composer Koichi Sugiyama and the Chunsoft team brought ideas from computer role-playing games to a console audience. A single hero explores the world and fights through menu commands. Its accessible presentation helped establish the form of the Japanese console RPG.

cards.heading: Reduce in Order to Make Readable
cards.text: Horii organised actions into menus and introduced enemies, equipment and goals gradually. Players could learn the commands while moving between towns and nearby dangers. Keeping the visible systems manageable gave people unfamiliar with computer RPGs a way into the adventure. New areas could then demand more of the same familiar actions.

cards.heading: The Journey Is Built on Distance from Enemies
cards.text: Random encounters consume health and magic as the hero travels. The farther a dungeon lies from a safe town, the more resources the journey may require. Better equipment helps defeat enemies and also allows longer expeditions before returning to recover. Numerical growth becomes visible on the map as places that once seemed out of reach become practical destinations.

cards.heading: Toriyama Makes the Monster Memorable Before Threatening
cards.text: Toriyama's monsters remain recognisable at the Famicom's small resolution. The Slime's simple outline and expressive face make an early enemy easy to identify and remember. Different creatures give battles a visual character alongside their numerical strengths. Some, especially the Slime, became lasting symbols of the series.
